newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat's wife says Netanyahu "does not like us".
newsitem.headline: Arafat's wife says Netanyahu "does not like us".

text.p: Yasser Arafat's wife Suha said in an interview published on Friday that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu did not like Palestinians nor peace deals with them.

The Israeli daily Yedioth Ahronoth quoted the Palestinian leader's wife saying her people were suffering under Israeli sanctions imposed after a bombing on a Jerusalem market, but that she would not "beg" the Netanyahu family for aid.
Mrs Arafat's remarks on Friday were in marked contrast to a warm defence she made one year ago of Netanyahu's wife Sara, who was having a rough time in the media, in the same newspaper.
"I know that he does not like us and does not like the accords," Yedioth quoted Mrs Arafat as saying during an interview at her Gaza home when asked about Netanyahu.
"Creativity, with great politicians like the deceased Rabin and Peres and my husband, is to learn to be flexible.... That has not happened with Netanyahu."
Netanyahu's immediate predecessors, Shimon Peres and Yitzhak Rabin, shared a Nobel Peace Prize with Arafat for their historic 1993 interim peace deal. Netanyahu opposed the deal.

Peres, who was Rabin's foreign minister, became prime minister after Rabin's 1995 assassination by a right-wing Jew. Netanyahu defeated Peres in 1996 elections but said he would keep signed peace deals.
After the July 30 bombing that killed 16 people, including the two attackers, Israel sealed off the West Bank and Gaza. It also withheld financial transfers it owed the Palestinians.
"There is suffering but we do not want your pity," Mrs Arafat told her Israeli interviewer, referring to tens of thousands of labourers who could not reach jobs in Israel.

"Too many children are dying of serious illnesses because we have not been able to transfer them for medical treatment outside Gaza," she added, saying she had a list of such cases. She did not present the list.
"But I do not intend to beg from the Netanyahu family," she said when asked why she did not personally ask for help.
Israel says it has allowed people with medical emergencies to travel for treatment despite the closure.

"These stories are obviously disinformation of the most despicable kind ... Every humanitarian case, every medical case is allowed to go through," Netanyahu's communications chief, David Bar-Illan, told Reuters. He refused to react to Mrs Arafat's statements concerning Netanyahu.
Since Netanyahu took office in June 1996, Israel-Palestinian relations have steadily deteriorated.
Negotiations between the sides broke down in March this year when Netanyahu launched a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem that Palestinians say pre-empted final peace talks.
The market bombing plunged ties deeper into crisis, with Netanyahu accusing Arafat of tacitly condoning militants. The identity of the bombers has yet to be established.
Arafat insists he is making a "100 percent effort" on security. He accuses Israel of using the bombing as a pretext to destroy the peace accords.
